findings.text: Request queue tail carries scheduler and freeze and debug state. It holds an elevator mutex, a sysfs mutex, a limits mutex, a list of unused hardware contexts with its spinlock, a freeze depth counter, a throttle pointer when throttling is enabled, an RCU head, optional lockdep freeze owner state, a freeze wait queue, a freeze mutex, a tag set pointer with tag set list, three debug dentries for queue and scheduler and QoS, and a debugfs mutex.

Elevator mutex guards scheduler switching, especially the elevator pointer. It also covers request count and write-back throttle latency attributes that elevator updates may change, plus hardware context tags, reserved tags and CPU mask attributes that hardware queue count updates may change. Required order for elevator or hardware queue count update is to freeze the queue first and then take this mutex.

Limits mutex guards queue limits and the read-ahead size attribute. A start helper takes this mutex and returns a copy of current limits for modification, while a cancel helper releases it without applying changes. Callers must hold it across limit updates.

Unused context spinlock guards the list used to reuse dead hardware contexts across hardware queue count changes. Freeze mutex serializes usage counter teardown and reinit against concurrent access. Debugfs mutex serializes all debug metadata operations that use the queue, scheduler and QoS dentries.

Queue flag indices in order are dying, nomerges, same completion, fail IO, no extended merges, same force, init done, stats, registered, quiesced, request alloc time, hardware context active, single-queue dispatch, disable write-back throttle default, no elevator switch, QoS enabled, bio issue time, zoned queue-depth-one writes, then a max sentinel marking the count.
Default multiqueue flag mask selects only the same completion flag bit.

Queue state predicates expose single flag tests for dying, init done, nomerges, no extended merges, quiesced, registered, single-queue dispatch, disable write-back throttle, no elevator switch, zoned queue-depth-one writes, and request alloc time recording. Each reports whether its corresponding queue flag is set.
Request alloc time reporting has two builds. One build tests the corresponding queue flag, the other build always reports false. The choice depends on build configuration not shown in the fragment.

Device capability predicates read queue limit feature bits for rotational, IO statistics, direct access, peer to peer DMA, skip tagset quiesce, and zoned. Zoned reporting additionally requires zoned support to be enabled at build time.

No-retry test reports whether a request carries any device, transport or driver fail-fast indication. Power-management-only state reads an atomic counter. Multiqueue detection reports whether the queue has multiqueue operations installed.
Runtime power status query has two builds. One returns the stored queue power status, the other always reports active. The selection depends on power management configuration.

Zoned helpers map sectors to zone numbers using the chunk size, expose maximum open and active zone limits, and report queue depth as the configured depth when nonzero else the request count. Zone count comes from the disk in zoned builds and is zero otherwise, with a block device wrapper delegating to its disk.
Default scatter-gather timeout is 60 HZ and minimum scatter-gather timeout is 7 HZ.

Bio iteration walks the chain of linked bios. Request lookup recovers the enclosing request from its queue list node. Vector mapping maps one bio vector page slice through DMA mapping with caller supplied direction and attributes.

Disk bring-up includes adding a disk with no parent and no groups, allocating a disk with caller limits and node plus a static lock class, and registering a block major with a name and no extra operations.

Block device flags live in an atomic word. Helpers extract the partition number, test a flag, set a flag, and clear a flag. Disk read-only combines the partition zero read-only flag with the disk read-only state, and device read-only combines its own flag with its disk state.

Geometry helpers expose start sector, sector count, byte size derived from sector count, disk capacity from partition zero, and filesystem block count derived by shifting sector count according to block size.

Zone write plugging is needed only when the disk has a plug hash, the operation is a write, empty flushes are excluded, the bio is not already marked as plugging, and the operation is one of zone append, write, write zeroes, zone finish, zone reset, or reset all. Other operations never need it.
Non-zoned builds stub out zoned behaviour. Zone count and sequential-zone test and plugging-need test and plug attempt all report false or zero without inspecting the device.
Zone capacity reports the last-zone capacity when the queried zone reaches or passes disk capacity, otherwise the regular zone capacity. A block device wrapper delegates to its disk.
Disk holder link and unlink in this build are no-operations. Link always reports success and unlink does nothing.
Poll one-shot flag occupies bit 0.

Bio zone number derives from its device disk and start sector. Straddle detection reports nonempty bios whose first and last sectors fall in different zones. Boundary helper reports remaining sectors to the next boundary, using masking for power-of-two boundaries and division otherwise.
Discard, secure erase and write zeroes can be disabled by clearing their maximum sector limits. Write zeroes disabling clears both regular and unmap limits.

Flush and block page counting in this build always report zero success. Filesystem discard and zero-out convert block ranges to sector ranges by shifting for block size and delegate to the underlying device operations, with zero-out using no extra flags.
Zeroing flags occupy bits 0, 1 and 2 for no unmap meaning do not free blocks, no fallback meaning do not write explicit zeroes, and killable meaning interruptible by fatal signals.
Default limits are 128 segments, 255 safe sectors, 65536 bytes maximum segment size, and a 32-bit all-ones segment boundary mask.

Limit accessors expose the queue limits object for a device, segment and virtual boundary masks, maximum sectors, a byte conversion capped before shifting, maximum hardware sectors, maximum segments, maximum discard segments, and maximum segment size.

Zone append is treated as emulated when the queue is zoned but has no hardware zone append limit, with a device wrapper. Related helpers expose maximum zone append sectors, maximum segments, and maximum write streams which is zero for partitions, plus a partition test based on nonzero partition number.
Geometry and granularity helpers expose physical block size, minimum and optimal IO sizes, and zone write granularity, each with queue and device forms where the device form delegates to its queue.
Device limit helpers expose maximum discard sectors, discard granularity, maximum secure erase sectors, maximum write zeroes sectors, and maximum write zeroes unmap sectors.

Write path attributes expose rotational, synchronous, integrity checksum presence requiring integrity support and a non-none checksum type, stable writes when checksum exists or the feature is set, write cache when the feature is set and not disabled, force unit access, no-wait, and zoned state, each via queue limits or queue wrappers.

Zone geometry helpers map sectors to zone numbers, report zone size in sectors as zero when not zoned else the chunk size, derive zone start by masking, derive offsets from zone start for devices and bios, and test zone start and zone alignment where alignment equals start.

DMA and atomic write helpers expose DMA alignment, maximum and minimum atomic write unit sizes, atomic boundary and maximum sizes converted from sectors to bytes, a device DMA alignment wrapper, a combined alignment and pad mask, a request alignment test on address and length, and a block size to bit count conversion.

Queue lifecycle moves through init done, registered and quiesced with dying marking teardown. Init done indicates initialization completed, registered indicates attachment to a disk, quiesced indicates suspended dispatch, and dying indicates teardown in progress.

Updating elevator or hardware queue count without freezing first violates the required order and risks races on request count, throttle latency and hardware context attributes visible through sysfs and debugfs. Limit changes outside the limits mutex risk races with readers of limits and read-ahead.

Skipping the zone plugging need test or the straddle check can misroute zone writes that must pass through the plug path. Capacity handling must use the tail capacity at the end of the device rather than the regular capacity.
